title: Planetary Nebula Sh2-290
caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-290, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: The bluish interior of Sh2-290 comes from energised oxygen atoms, and one side of the nebula is noticeably brighter than the rest. This is an ancient planetary nebula in the constellation Cancer.
A planetary nebula forms when a star of low mass throws off its outer layers as it dies. Sh2-290 is among the largest planetary nebulae known.

Its lopsided brightness has an explanation: on that side, the nebula is running into the thin interstellar gas around it, and the collision makes it glow more strongly. Old planetary nebulae like this one have had time to expand a long way, so their surroundings play a bigger part in shaping them. Different elements in the gas each glow at their own colours, which is how the oxygen in the interior can be picked out.
scale: Sh2-290 has a diameter of about 7 parsecs, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red, sulphur [S II] in cyan and oxygen [O III] in blue.
